question: On 28 September 2026, Bergamo Province filed Decree No 275 concerning appeal No 813/2026 R.G., brought by Montello S.p.A. before the Lombardy’s Regional Administrative Court seeking the annulment of an environmental notice1.

Given the presence, within a radius of just 30 kilometres, of three incinerators and a cement plant that practices co-combustion, and given the importance of the plant, its full compliance with the Industrial Emissions Directive (IED) and the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive (EIA) needs to be verified. In view of the above: 1.

Can the Commission check whether the Italian authorities’ integrated environmental permits and checks comply with the IED and the EIA, paying particular attention to the requirements concerning odour emissions and best available techniques?
If it does appear that EU law has been breached, what steps will it take against Italy to ensure that EU law is correctly applied?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.11.2026) Under the Industrial Emissions Directive (IED)1, installations must operate in accordance with their permit conditions, including the use of best available techniques (BAT) and compliance with emission levels. Where relevant, this may also include provisions addressing odour, in line with the applicable BAT Conclusions2.
Under the IED, competent national authorities are responsible for ensuring compliance with permit conditions.

Under the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive3, Member States must ensure that, before they are authorised, certain projects likely to have significant effects on the environment by virtue, inter alia, of their nature, size or location are made subject to an assessment of the environmental effects.

Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, compliance with EU law falls primarily with the national authorities, including judicial ones, who are better placed to assess individual situations such as the one referred to by the Honourable Member, and intervene if necessary.

Moreover, the IED and EIA Directives, as transposed into Italian law, contain specific provisions related to access to justice. The Commission, for its part, ensures that EU rules are correctly transposed at national level and prioritises its enforcement efforts on cases pointing to a systemic breach of EU law4.
1 Directive 2010/75/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 November 2010 on industrial and

livestock rearing emissions (integrated pollution prevention and control), OJ L 334, 17.12.2010, pp. 17–119. 2 Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2019/2010 of 12 November 2019 establishing the best available techniques (BAT) conclusions, under Directive 2010/75/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council, for waste incineration, OJ L 312, 3.12.2019, pp. 55–91.

3 Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the assessment of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment, OJ L 26, 28.1.2012, pp. 1–21. 4 https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-making-process/better-regulation/simplification-implementationenforcement/simpler-clearer-and-better-enforced-eu-rulebook_en.
